source: Nominees sourced from Wikipedia per-state race articles (permalinked), cross-checked against FEC candidate filings.

races.note: Alaska uses a top-four nonpartisan primary; two Republicans (Sullivan, Heikes) advanced. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. (Undeclared, certified on the general ballot) is not shown in this version.

Bob Chew (Forward Party) reported ~$3.6M raised, far outpacing minor rivals — included as provisional pending the real independent-expenditure check in prompt 2b, but worth separate confirmation of his seriousness as a contender.

Special election for the seat Marco Rubio vacated; Ashley Moody was appointed and is the Republican nominee. Neil J. Gillespie's ballot qualification is ambiguous in the source (listed "Declared" but also appears in the results table) — flagged for confirmation.
No Libertarian on the ballot this cycle per contemporaneous AJC reporting cited in the source article.
Democrat David Roth withdrew; party fielded no replacement, so there is no Democratic nominee this cycle. Todd Achilles (independent, former Democratic state rep) is the main challenger to Risch.

Louisiana eliminated its jungle primary for this cycle (traditional party primaries + runoffs, effective 2026). Incumbent Bill Cassidy was eliminated in his own primary. Confirmed independently via AP/local news (WAFB, Fox8, KNOE): Letlow and Davis are the only two general-election nominees.
Graham Platner won the Democratic track but withdrew; Troy Jackson was chosen as replacement nominee at a July 25 convention.

Ballot status for the four minor-party candidates below was not fully confirmed from the fetched article text (they appeared in a "Third parties and independents" section, not a certified results table) — flagged for your review.

Peggy Flanagan is a nickname for Margaret Flanagan (her FEC filing name) — fuzzy name matching required. Rebecca Whiting's party is labeled "Libertarian" in the results table but "(G)"/Green in a polling footnote elsewhere in the same article — discrepancy unresolved, flagged.
Ty Pinkins withdrew from the Democratic primary and is running as an independent; reported ~$104K raised and 6-7% polling as of mid-October.

Steve Daines withdrew from the primary at the filing deadline and endorsed Kurt Alme, who became the GOP nominee (replacement). Seth Bodnar (independent) is treated as a serious three-way contender by the source.
Seven declared independents are explicitly listed as "Disqualified" by the source and are excluded.

Democratic primary winner Cindy Burbank withdrew; a lawsuit to force a replacement nominee was dismissed, so there is no Democratic nominee. Dan Osborn (independent) is the main challenger. Mike Marvin withdrew/endorsed Osborn but remains printed on the ballot per source.
Eduardo Castillo is a write-in only and is excluded per the write-in exclusion rule.

Larry Marker was nominated via write-in in the Republican primary (unusual path, but he is the confirmed general-election R nominee). Mira O'Connell (independent) is listed as not qualifying and is excluded.

Special election for the seat JD Vance vacated; Jon Husted was appointed and is the Republican nominee. Greg Levy is reportedly a Party for Socialism and Liberation member filing as an independent — label mismatch flagged.

Ron Meinhardt and Curtis Stinnett's formal ballot qualification as independents was not confirmed in the fetched article text (only a results table and campaign links were visible) — flagged for your review.
Chris Henry has a Progressive ballot line and a cross-nomination from the Pacific Green Party per source.
Michael Bahry's formal ballot qualification was not confirmed in the fetched article text — flagged for your review.

Incumbent Lindsey Graham died in July 2026; Gov. McMaster appointed his sister Darline Graham, who then won the Republican nomination (confirmed via WRDW news: "4 candidates set for South Carolina's US Senate race in November" — Graham, Andrews, Whitener, Hackett — independently corroborating the Wikipedia source). I attempted the SC Election Commission's own site directly but could not find a fetchable certified-candidate page; the Wikipedia source plus independent news cross-check is the basis for this entry.
Democratic nominee Julian Beaudion won unopposed but withdrew in August, leaving no Democratic nominee. Brian Bengs (independent, 2022 Democratic nominee) is the main challenger to Rounds.

Source lists nine additional independent filers (Chandler, Gerena, Hearn, Jones, Macon III, Matthews, Sutman Jr., Whitson, and Mixon with an inconsistent party label) with no indication of serious candidacy or campaign activity. Excluded from this list pending the real independent-expenditure check in prompt 2b — flagged in the excluded-filers table rather than included here, since nothing in the source suggests they meet the inclusion bar.
Incumbent John Cornyn lost the Republican primary to Ken Paxton — a primary-level event, not a general-election replacement.
